title: Show missing or blocked data as unavailable, never as zero
hypothesis: If every report shows a missing or blocked value as unavailable instead of 0, then fewer budget and stock calls get made on a false zero.

signal.check: A report, dashboard or card shows a blank field, an empty coupon or promotion card, or a threshold-suppressed value as 0 or blank instead of a clear label.

risk.note: None. This only changes how a value is labelled, not the data itself.

prerequisites: A reporting template or script that builds the store's regular reports
steps: List every place a report can show 0: empty GA4 cards, blank Meta CAPI fields, a Shopify metric the plan does not expose.
Change the report or script so a missing input prints unavailable, not 0.
Read (not set) in GA4 as unknown, and report its share instead of dropping it.
Re-check the next report to confirm no 0 hides a missing input.

test.method: Run the next scheduled report and check every metric column by hand against its raw source
test.measure: count of rows where unavailable replaced a former silent 0

title: End every analytics report with a decision, not a status update
hypothesis: If every report closes with a named action, then fewer reports get read and filed without changing what the store does.

signal.check: The store's last few reports end with a chart or a number and no action line, or say only keep monitoring.

risk.note: None; this is a template change.

prerequisites: A standing report or dashboard the store already reviews
steps: Add a required last line to every report template: the decision this supports (restock, pause, scale, change offer, fix a step, or keep as is).
Show comparative series (revenue against AOV, profit, new customers, channel) instead of a single revenue line.
Reject a draft report that ends without a named action.

test.method: Review the next 5 reports produced against the template
test.measure: share of reports with a stated decision line

title: Pick one source of truth per question and write it down
hypothesis: If the store names one tool as the answer for each type of question, then teams stop arguing over GA4 vs Shopify numbers that were never meant to match.

signal.check: Two tools report the same thing (GA4 sessions vs Shopify sessions, GA4 revenue vs Shopify revenue) and the team keeps trying to reconcile them exactly.

risk.note: A wrong pick can be changed later; log the change date.

prerequisites: Access to the store platform, GA4 and any finance report used for cash
steps: List the store's 5 to 10 most asked measurement questions (traffic source, order count, cash on hand, per-page conversion).
Assign one tool per question: store platform for orders and sales totals, GA4 for traffic source and per-page conversion, payments report for cash.
Write the list in the brand record and stop trying to force GA4 and Shopify numbers to match exactly.

test.method: Check the written source-of-truth list against the next 3 team questions that come up
test.measure: share of questions answered from the assigned source without a side debate

title: Start logging data before you know if it matters
hypothesis: If the store logs order attributes, survey answers and cost lines from day one, then later analysis is not blocked by history that was never captured.

signal.check: The store cannot answer a basic history question (cost per acquisition before paid ads started, past survey answers, past refund dates) because it was never logged.

risk.note: None; logging more does not remove any existing capability.

steps: List data that might matter later: order attributes, survey answers, funnel step counts, refund dates, all acquisition costs before paid ads.
Turn on logging or exports for each item now, even with no current use.
Store the logs somewhere the team can query later, not only in a tool's own short-retention UI.

test.method: Check in 90 days whether the logged data answers a question that came up
test.measure: number of questions answerable from logged history

title: Size the analytics setup to the store's own ad spend, not a big brand's
hypothesis: If a small store matches its measurement effort to its spend and headcount, then time is not lost building a data stack a bigger brand needs.

signal.check: The team is spending founder or agency hours on a tool, dashboard or process sized for a much bigger ad budget than the store runs.

risk.note: Under-investing in tracking too long is the opposite risk; revisit as spend grows.

prerequisites: Current monthly ad spend and current analyst or founder hours on measurement
steps: Write down current monthly spend and who spends time on measurement.
Match the setup to that tier: a low-spend store needs GA4, pixel and CAPI working and a daily trust check, not a data warehouse.
Set a spend threshold at which to revisit (add headcount, add tools) and log it.

test.method: Compare hours spent on measurement against hours spent on offers, creative and ops
test.measure: share of team time on measurement vs revenue-facing work

title: Cut the capture day from spend tables and flag any single row that swings the total
hypothesis: If every ROAS or CPA table drops the partial capture day and flags rows that move the total a lot, then the store stops reacting to a fake spike or crash from one order.

signal.check: A spend, ROAS or CPA table includes today or the last cached day, or a single row with tiny spend and one order swings the whole period's ratio.

risk.note: None; this only changes which days and rows a table includes.

prerequisites: A script or export that builds spend and ROAS tables
steps: In the reporting script, drop the capture day and any day the source marks partial before computing totals.
State the window as from date to date, last full day, on every table.
Flag any single row whose spend-to-result ratio is far from the table's average (for example one order on very low spend).

test.method: Re-run the last ROAS table with the fix applied and compare to the original
test.measure: change in the period ROAS number and number of flagged rows

title: Keep one GA4 account per business, never merge two brands into one
hypothesis: If each business gets its own GA4 account, then one brand's data never leaks into or gets confused with another's.

signal.check: An agency or multi-brand owner is running more than one brand's properties inside a single shared GA4 account to save setup time.

risk.note: Moving an existing property to a new account loses its history; plan a cut-over date rather than editing live.

prerequisites: Admin access to Google Analytics
steps: Check whether more than one brand's properties sit inside one GA4 account.
If so, create a separate account for each business going forward.
Log the cut-over date for any property that moves.

test.method: Audit the GA4 account list once
test.measure: number of brands per GA4 account

title: Give one shopper journey one GA4 property, and list every domain it touches
hypothesis: If every domain a shopper crosses before buying sits under one GA4 property and is listed in Configure your domains, then the journey is not split into fake separate sessions.

signal.check: The store checkout, storefront or a subscription portal runs on a second domain that is missing from the GA4 property's Configure your domains list.

risk.note: Adding a domain to the list does not affect past data.

prerequisites: List of every domain a shopper touches from landing to thank-you page
steps: List every domain a shopper can land on, browse or check out on before a purchase completes.
Confirm all of them share one GA4 property, unless one is a fully separate business line.
Admin > Data streams > web stream > Configure tag settings > Configure your domains: add every root domain.
Save and confirm cross-domain sessions no longer break at the domain change.

test.method: Walk a full purchase across domains in DebugView after the change
test.measure: whether the walk stays in one session

title: Keep one web data stream per GA4 property
hypothesis: If the store keeps a single web stream even when several sites share one journey, then Tech reports stay clean instead of splitting traffic across streams that should be one.

signal.check: Tech > Platform shows less than 100% Web on a web-only property, or more than one web stream exists for one journey.

risk.note: Merging streams later needs a new stream setup; check before removing an old one.

prerequisites: Admin access to GA4
steps: Check Admin > Data streams for more than one web stream on the same property.
Keep one web stream for the web journey; give a native app its own stream.
Recheck Tech > Platform reads 100% Web on a web-only property once data arrives.

test.method: Check Tech > Platform after the change
test.measure: share of sessions reading as Web
test.read_point: 24 to 48 hours after any stream change

title: Lock GA4 time zone and currency at property creation and never change time zone later
hypothesis: If time zone and currency are set correctly at creation and time zone is never changed after, then the store avoids a data gap or overlap that cannot be cleanly fixed.

signal.check: A GA4 property's time zone or currency does not match the store's business time zone and store currency, or someone plans to change the time zone on a live property.

risk.note: A wrong time zone found after data arrives cannot be fixed cleanly; the fix is a new property, not an edit.

prerequisites: Business time zone and store currency confirmed
steps: Confirm the store's business time zone and store currency before creating any property.
Set both at property creation (Admin > Property Details for existing properties, cannot change time zone later).
If a property already has the wrong time zone, create a new property and log the cut-over date instead of editing the live one.

test.method: Check Property Details against the brand record
test.measure: match between property settings and store's real time zone and currency

title: Pick the GA4 business objective that unlocks the full report set
hypothesis: If the property picks the business objective that includes every standard report, then the team is not missing report tabs it needs later.

signal.check: At property creation a narrow business objective was chosen and some standard report tabs seem to be missing.

risk.note: The report menu can be changed later in Library by an editor or admin.

steps: At property creation, pick the broadest business objective option to get the fullest report set.
If an existing property looks narrow, open Library (editor or admin access) and adjust the report collections shown.

test.method: Check the Reports menu after setup for the expected tabs
test.measure: presence of expected report sections

title: Review GA4's automatic events at setup and turn off form interactions
hypothesis: If the team reviews all 7 automatic GA4 events at stream creation instead of accepting the defaults, then unwanted or unreliable events do not clutter reports.

signal.check: A stream's enhanced measurement settings were never opened after creation, or form_interaction events are on without a reason.

risk.note: Toggling these off only stops future collection of that event type.

prerequisites: Admin access to the GA4 data stream
steps: Open the stream's enhanced measurement settings before or right after stream creation.
Turn off form interactions.
Review the other 6 (page views, scrolls, outbound clicks, site search, video, file downloads) and turn off any the brand does not want.
Save and confirm the choice in the brand record.

test.method: Check DebugView for the events after the change
test.measure: which automatic events still fire

title: Install GA4 through GTM on storefront pages; use the platform's own route for checkout
hypothesis: If GA4 is installed through GTM on storefront pages and through the platform's own integration on checkout, then more pages get tracked without breaking the parts a hosted checkout blocks.
does_not_apply_when: A fully custom checkout with developer access can run GTM everywhere and skip the platform route

signal.check: GTM is live on some pages, but checkout or thank-you events are missing, or checkout runs on a platform such as Shopify that blocks GTM.

risk.note: Publishing a new route can be reverted with a GTM version rollback.

prerequisites: Know the store platform and whether checkout is hosted
A GTM container created for the storefront
steps: Confirm whether checkout is hosted by the platform or fully custom.
If hosted, note GTM cannot fire inside checkout; use the platform's native app or pixel there.
Install GTM on every storefront page you control, for GA4 and other vendor tags.
Confirm in DebugView that checkout and purchase events still arrive from the native route.

test.method: Walk the full journey from storefront to checkout to thank-you page in DebugView
test.measure: which route each event arrived from

title: Test every new or changed tag in GTM Preview and GA4 DebugView before publishing
hypothesis: If every tag change is proven in both GTM Preview and GA4 DebugView before it is published, then broken or half-firing tags stop reaching production.

signal.check: A tag was published without checking that it fired in Preview and that GA4 received it with correct parameters in DebugView.

risk.note: GTM keeps versions; publish the previous version if a bad tag ships.

prerequisites: GTM Preview and GA4 DebugView access
steps: Build or change the tag in GTM but do not publish yet.
Open GTM Preview, connect to the site, and confirm the tag fired at the right trigger.
Open GA4 DebugView, find the event, and check every parameter, not only the event name.
Only after both pass, publish with a clear version name.

test.method: Repeat the same Preview and DebugView check after every future tag change
test.measure: share of published tags that passed both checks first

title: Wait for GA4 processing before reading standard reports after any change
hypothesis: If the team waits 24 to 48 hours after a new install, event or dimension before reading standard reports, then early numbers are not mistaken for the fully processed picture.

signal.check: Someone reads a standard GA4 report the same day as a new install, a new event, or a new custom dimension and treats it as final.

expected_effect.size: wait 24 to 48 hours (one source says 12 to 24); keep the stricter 48 hours

risk.note: None; this is a waiting rule, not a change to data.

steps: After any new install, event, or custom dimension, note the date and time.
Use Realtime and DebugView only to confirm arrival in the first 48 hours.
Do not read or act on standard reports until 48 hours have passed.

test.method: Compare a report read at 24 hours against the same report read at 48 hours
test.measure: how much the numbers move between the two reads

title: Use lowercase underscore event names and register every custom parameter
hypothesis: If every custom event uses a lowercase underscore name and every parameter is registered as a custom dimension, then those events actually show up and can be filtered in reports.

signal.check: A custom event name has capitals or spaces, or a custom parameter never appears as a usable column or filter in GA4.

risk.note: Custom dimensions cannot be deleted quickly, only archived, once created.

prerequisites: A custom event already built in GTM
steps: Name every custom event in lowercase with underscores, matching exactly across GTM, GA4 and any filter.
After the event fires in DebugView, note every parameter it carries.
Admin > Custom definitions > create a custom dimension for each parameter, using the exact key and event scope.
Confirm the dimension appears as a usable column in a free form exploration.

test.method: Build a one-off exploration filtered to the event and check every parameter shows a value
test.measure: number of parameters visible vs sent

title: Define and activate an internal traffic filter for office, warehouse and agency IPs
hypothesis: If staff and agency visits are filtered out by IP, then reports stop counting internal testing as real customer sessions.
does_not_apply_when: The whole team works from home with no static IP to filter

signal.check: The internal traffic filter in Admin > Data filters shows Testing instead of Active, or no rule exists for office, warehouse or agency IPs.

risk.note: Filters apply forward only; there is nothing to undo in past data.

prerequisites: needs brand data: office, warehouse and agency static IPs
steps: Get every static IP used by staff, warehouse and any agency touching the site.
Configure tag settings > Define internal traffic > create a rule per IP.
Go to Data filters, find the internal traffic filter, and switch it from Testing to Active.
Recheck after a week that internal sessions are excluded, not just labelled.

test.method: Visit the site from a listed office IP and check the session is excluded or tagged internal
test.measure: whether the internal filter marks or drops that session

title: Set GA4 event data retention to 14 months on day one
hypothesis: If retention is set to 14 months right when the property is created, then the store can compare this year's peak season to last year's instead of losing the history.

signal.check: A GA4 property still shows the 2-month default retention in Admin > Data retention.

risk.note: Extending retention going forward is safe; data already lost under the 2-month default cannot be recovered.

steps: Open Admin > Data retention on the property.
Change event data retention from 2 months to 14 months.
Save immediately, before any other setting change, since this cannot be applied retroactively.

test.method: Check Admin > Data retention shows 14 months
test.measure: retention setting value

title: Decide and log the GA4 session timeout instead of leaving it on autopilot
hypothesis: If the brand makes a written, dated decision on session timeout instead of an accidental change, then session counts stay comparable across GA4, Shopify and ad platforms.

signal.check: The session timeout was changed from the 30-minute default without a written decision and a logged date, or nobody has ever reviewed it.

expected_effect.size: a longer timeout can cut (not set) landing pages and false checkout landing pages, per one source's opinion

risk.note: A longer timeout merges same-day visits and changes session counts, breaking comparability with history.

steps: Check the current session timeout under Configure tag settings > Adjust session timeout.
Decide as a brand: keep the 30-minute default for comparability with Shopify and ad platforms, or extend it for fewer false checkout landing pages.
If changed, log the date and reason in the brand record.
Annotate every report that spans the change date.

test.method: Compare session counts and per-session conversion rate for 2 weeks before and after any change
test.measure: session count and conversion rate shift

title: Decide and log the GA4 engaged-session timer instead of changing it casually
hypothesis: If the brand makes a written decision on the engaged-session timer and never compares engagement rate across a change, then engagement rate stays a trustworthy signal over time.

signal.check: The 10-second engaged session timer was changed without a logged decision, or engagement rate is compared across a period that crossed a timer change.

risk.note: Changing the timer breaks engagement rate comparisons across the change date.

steps: Check the current engaged session timer (default 10 seconds).
Decide as a brand whether to raise it; one source raises it to 30 seconds or more by preference, with no measured benefit.
Log the decision and date if changed.
Never compare engagement rate across the change date without noting it.

test.method: Track engagement rate for 2 weeks before and after any change
test.measure: engagement rate shift

title: Turn on Google Signals only after a consent review for every selling country
hypothesis: If Google Signals is enabled only after checking consent rules in every selling country, then the store avoids collecting demographic data it is not allowed to collect.

signal.check: Google Signals is on, or being considered, without a documented consent review for each country the store sells to.

expected_effect.size: demographics may take weeks to populate and are directional only

risk.note: Signals can be turned off again, but data already collected under an unreviewed setting cannot be undone.

prerequisites: needs brand data: selling countries and their consent rules
steps: List every country the store sells to and its consent rules.
Get a consent review before enabling Signals in any of those markets.
If cleared, go to Admin > Data collection > Google Signals data collection and turn it on.
Log the decision and expect several weeks before demographic data appears.

test.method: Check demographic reports 3 to 4 weeks after enabling
test.measure: whether demographic data has populated and consent stayed compliant

title: Run the 5-point GA4 settings audit in order: retention, domains, filter, timing, Signals
hypothesis: If the team always checks retention first, then domains, then internal traffic, then timeout and timer, then Signals, then the setting that cannot be recovered gets fixed before anything else.

signal.check: A new or existing GA4 property has not had all 5 settings checked in this order, especially retention.

risk.note: This is a checklist order, not a change by itself.

prerequisites: A new or existing GA4 property
steps: Check retention first, since it cannot be recovered if missed.
Check every domain is listed under Configure your domains.
Check the internal traffic filter is Active, not Testing.
Decide and log session timeout and engaged timer, or confirm they are still on a logged decision.
Decide Google Signals after a consent review.

test.method: Run the 5-point checklist on this property and any new one
test.measure: number of the 5 settings that pass
test.read_point: at setup and every quarterly audit

title: Link Google Ads and Search Console under GA4 Product Links when the brand runs them
hypothesis: If Google Ads and Search Console are linked under Product Links, then the store gets Ads conversion imports and Search Console data inside GA4 instead of working from 2 separate tools.
does_not_apply_when: The store runs neither Google Ads nor treats organic search as a priority

signal.check: The store runs Google Ads or cares about organic search, but Product Links shows no Google Ads or Search Console connection.

risk.note: Unlinking later is straightforward and does not affect past data.

prerequisites: Admin access to both GA4 and the Google Ads or Search Console account
steps: Confirm the brand runs Google Ads, uses Search Console, or both.
Admin > Product Links > link Google Ads if it runs.
Admin > Product Links > link Search Console if organic search matters.
Confirm the Advertising section starts showing linked conversions.

test.method: Check the Advertising section for Google Ads data after linking
test.measure: presence of linked conversion data

title: Set up Consent Settings before using EU user data for Google Ads targeting
hypothesis: If Consent Settings is configured and consent mode is detected before EU user data is used for Ads targeting, then the store avoids using data it does not have permission to use.
does_not_apply_when: The store sells to no EU markets and runs no EU-targeted ads

signal.check: The store targets EU users with Google Ads and Admin > Data collection shows consent mode is not detected.

risk.note: Using EU data for Ads targeting without proper consent is a compliance risk, not only a data quality one.

prerequisites: needs brand data: markets served
web check: consent mode v2 setup for the store's platform and markets
steps: Confirm whether the store sells to or targets ads at EU users.
Check Admin > Data collection and modification > Consent Settings for consent mode detection.
If not detected, set up consent mode v2 for the store's platform before using EU data for Ads targeting.
Log the setup date.

test.method: Check the Consent Settings status after setup
test.measure: whether consent mode reads as detected

title: Confirm every ecommerce event arrives before trusting any funnel or revenue report
hypothesis: If view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout and purchase are confirmed arriving with real data before any report is trusted, then a missing event stops being mistaken for a real drop in behavior.

signal.check: A funnel or monetization report looks empty or has a step at zero, and nobody has walked a real order through DebugView to confirm every ecommerce event fires.

risk.note: This is a check; it only becomes risky if a real gap is found and left unfixed.

prerequisites: DebugView access
A test order path that will not create a real charge, or a real order that will be refunded
steps: Record which route sends each page type's events: storefront, checkout, thank-you page.
Open DebugView and walk a full journey: collection page, product page, add to cart, begin checkout, add shipping, add payment, purchase.
For each step, record whether the event name and its parameters (value, currency, items, transaction_id) arrived.
Mark each step pass, fail or unknown, and write the fix list with an owner for every gap.

test.method: Repeat the DebugView walk after any fix
test.measure: number of steps marked pass

title: Mark purchase, with a unique transaction ID, as the only sales key event
hypothesis: If purchase with a unique transaction_id is the only event marked as the sales key event, then a reload or a thank-you page revisit stops inflating the sale count.

signal.check: A thank-you page view, not the purchase event, is marked as the sales key event, or purchase events lack a unique transaction_id.

expected_effect.size: removes double counting from reloads and revisits

risk.note: Unmarking a key event does not stop the event from collecting.

prerequisites: Ecommerce event coverage confirmed
steps: Admin > Events > find purchase in the list.
Mark it as a key event. If purchase is missing, stop and fix event coverage first.
Confirm in DebugView that purchase carries transaction_id, value, currency and items.
Never use a thank-you page URL match as the sales key event; reserve that method for lead forms only.

test.method: Check the Purchases predefined audience for users after a test purchase
test.measure: whether the audience is non-empty

title: Mark only real business outcomes as key events, never page_view
hypothesis: If only true outcomes, such as purchase or a real lead, are marked as key events and page_view never is, then key event rates keep meaning something instead of being diluted.

signal.check: page_view or another non-outcome event is marked as a key event.

risk.note: Unmarking a key event does not remove the underlying data.

steps: Open Admin > Events > Key Events and list everything currently marked.
Remove page_view or any other non-outcome event from the key event list.
For a lead outcome with no event of its own, create a unique event first, then mark it.

test.method: Recheck the key event list
test.measure: number of non-outcome events still marked

title: Decide and log how leads are counted: once per session or once per event
hypothesis: If the brand picks and logs one counting method for lead key events, then lead volume is not silently over- or under-counted by a default nobody chose.

signal.check: A lead key event uses the default counting method without anyone deciding whether once-per-session fits the brand's lead flow better.

risk.note: Changing the counting method later breaks comparability with past periods.

prerequisites: A lead key event already created
steps: Open the lead event's settings and find the counting option (once per event vs once per session).
Decide which fits: once per event for a form that can be meaningfully submitted more than once; once per session otherwise.
Log the decision and date.

test.method: Compare lead counts under both settings for a week if unsure
test.measure: lead count difference

title: Filter every conversion rate to purchase and label the denominator
hypothesis: If every conversion rate reported to a person is filtered to purchase and labelled with its denominator, then nobody mistakes a mixed key-event rate for the real purchase rate.

signal.check: A conversion rate or key event rate shown in a report or deck is not filtered to purchase, or does not say what session count it is based on.

expected_effect.size: one example store read 1.7 percent only after applying the purchase filter, versus a higher unfiltered number

risk.note: None; this changes the report filter, not the data.

steps: In every acquisition or landing page report, set the key event rate selector to purchase.
Add the denominator (session count) as a labelled column next to the rate.
Recheck this filter after any change to the key event list.

test.method: Check the last conversion rate reported against a raw, unfiltered pull
test.measure: difference between filtered and unfiltered rate

title: Report Purchase Revenue for sales, not Total Revenue
hypothesis: If sales figures come from Purchase Revenue instead of Total Revenue, then a non-purchase event carrying a value parameter cannot quietly inflate the sales number.

signal.check: GA4's Total Revenue and Purchase Revenue differ in Monetization Overview and nobody has explained the gap.

risk.note: None; this is a reporting choice.

steps: Open Monetization Overview and compare Total Revenue to Purchase Revenue.
If they differ, list every event that sends a value parameter besides purchase.
Use Purchase Revenue as the sales number in every report.

test.method: Recheck the two figures next period
test.measure: size of any remaining unexplained gap

title: Expect GA4 key events and Google Ads conversions to differ, and explain the gap
hypothesis: If the team checks Conversion management to see both counts and explains the difference, then nobody wastes time trying to force GA4 key events to equal Google Ads conversions.
does_not_apply_when: The store does not run Google Ads

signal.check: Someone is confused or alarmed that GA4 key events do not match Google Ads conversions after linking the accounts.

risk.note: None; this is a reading habit, not a setting.

prerequisites: Google Ads linked to GA4
steps: Open Conversion management and list both GA4 key events and Google Ads conversion actions.
Identify any Ads-only conversion actions that explain the gap.
Note the explanation next to any report that shows both counts.

test.method: Recheck after adding or removing a conversion action
test.measure: whether the gap stays explained
test.read_point: after any change to conversion actions

title: Register the ecommerce parameters you plan to report on, like coupon and item list
hypothesis: If coupon, item_list_name, promotion and other custom fields are actually sent and registered, then their Monetization cards stop showing empty by default.

signal.check: The coupon, promotion or item list cards in Monetization Overview are empty even though the store uses coupons, promotions or product lists.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: web check: GA4 recommended ecommerce events and parameters
steps: Check Monetization Overview for empty coupon, promotion or item list cards.
Confirm with a developer or the app whether those parameters are actually sent on the relevant events.
Add the missing parameters to the event payload.
Register any new custom parameter as a custom dimension.

test.method: Recheck Monetization Overview after the fix
test.measure: whether the cards populate

title: Track cart and checkout abandonment as its own stage, separate from the purchase funnel
hypothesis: If abandoned carts and checkouts are tracked as their own stage with a clear time window, then recovery emails and texts have a real trigger instead of a guess.

signal.check: begin_checkout or add_to_cart events are confirmed arriving, but nothing defines when a cart or checkout counts as abandoned.

risk.note: None; this is additional tracking, not a change to existing events.

prerequisites: begin_checkout and add_to_cart confirmed arriving
needs brand data: abandoned cart definition and time window
steps: Confirm add_to_cart and begin_checkout events are arriving.
Define the store's abandonment window, for example 1 hour with no purchase.
Build the abandonment view or segment on top of these events, separate from the purchase funnel.
Hand the recovery send timing and copy to the email and SMS lifecycle track.

test.method: Compare abandonment counts against known recovery flow trigger counts
test.measure: match rate between the two

title: Add a renewal event for a subscription store and read churn by cancellation date
hypothesis: If a subscription store tracks a renewal event and reads churn by cancellation date, then churn is not confused with a one-off failed card.

signal.check: A subscription or recurring-revenue store has no renewal event with value, currency and subscription id, or reads churn from failed payments instead of cancellation date.

risk.note: None; this adds tracking, it does not change billing.

steps: Confirm the subscription platform can fire a renewal event with value, currency and subscription id.
Add the renewal event next to the purchase event.
Define churn as a customer cancellation, not a failed card retry.
Build a churn report keyed on cancellation date.

test.method: Compare churn counted by cancellation date against churn counted by failed payment for one month
test.measure: difference in churn rate between the two methods

title: Tag a post-purchase upsell as its own event so it does not inflate AOV
hypothesis: If a post-purchase upsell or cross-sell fires its own event instead of folding into the first order, then AOV reporting reflects the original order, not a combined number.

signal.check: The store runs a post-purchase upsell or cross-sell offer, and its revenue is not separated from the original order's AOV.

risk.note: None; this only changes how revenue is split in reporting.

prerequisites: The store runs a post-purchase upsell or cross-sell offer
steps: Confirm the post-purchase offer app or flow fires a separate event or order for the upsell.
If it currently merges into the original order, work with the developer or app settings to split it.
Report original-order AOV and upsell revenue as 2 separate lines.

test.method: Compare AOV before and after separating upsell revenue
test.measure: change in reported AOV

title: Confirm item-level parameters arrive on every ecommerce event
hypothesis: If item_id, item_name, price and quantity are confirmed present on every ecommerce event, then product-level reports do not silently break even though the event itself fires.

signal.check: An ecommerce event like add_to_cart or purchase fires, but its items array is missing item_id, item_name, price or quantity in DebugView.

risk.note: None; this is a check, not a change.

prerequisites: Ecommerce events confirmed arriving
steps: Open DebugView on a test purchase or add-to-cart.
Open the event's items array and check item_id, item_name, price and quantity are all present.
If any is missing, log it as a fix with an owner, developer or app settings.

test.method: Recheck the items array after the fix
test.measure: share of item fields present

title: Check the GA4 Purchases audience has users after purchase tracking is set up
hypothesis: If the Purchases predefined audience shows real users, then the purchase event and key event marking are confirmed working end to end.

signal.check: The Purchases predefined audience in Admin > Audiences is empty even though the store has real orders.

risk.note: None; this is a check.

prerequisites: purchase marked as a key event
steps: Open Admin > Audiences and find the Purchases predefined audience.
Check it has users matching recent order volume.
If empty, re-check that purchase is sent, marked as a key event, and carries a value.

test.method: Recheck the audience count weekly
test.measure: audience size vs known order count

title: Use Traffic acquisition, not User acquisition, to judge channel spend
hypothesis: If a spend or channel decision reads Traffic acquisition instead of User acquisition, then credit lands on the session that actually happened this period, not on whoever first brought the user in ever.

signal.check: A budget or channel-kill decision is being made from User acquisition (first touch ever), which mixes in sessions from channels that ran months ago.

risk.note: None; this is a report choice.

steps: Before reading any channel spend question, ask: is this about this period's sessions, or about who first brought the customer in?
Use Traffic acquisition for a spend or budget question.
Use User acquisition only for a brand or lifetime-value question.
Note in the report which report was used and why.

test.method: Pull the same channel question from both reports and compare the numbers
test.measure: size of the gap between User and Traffic acquisition reads

title: Read channel group, then medium, then campaign, in that order
hypothesis: If reads always drill from channel group to medium to campaign, then a named sender or ad set that channel group alone hides gets found before budget moves.

signal.check: A channel decision is made from the top-level channel group alone, without checking medium or campaign underneath it.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: UTMs applied per the brand convention
steps: Open Traffic acquisition with Session primary channel group as the first dimension.
Add Session medium as a second dimension.
Add Session campaign name as a third dimension to see which specific campaign drove sessions and revenue.
Sort by sessions or revenue before drawing a conclusion.

test.method: Compare a channel-only read against the same period drilled to campaign
test.measure: whether the campaign-level read changes the conclusion

title: Customize and save GA4 report tables instead of reading the defaults
hypothesis: If the team builds and saves a report table with the exact columns the question needs, then every recurring read stops missing the purchase filter or the revenue column.

signal.check: The team reads a GA4 report's default columns instead of a saved table built for the store's usual questions.

risk.note: None.

steps: List the metrics the store checks most: sessions, engaged sessions, engagement rate, key events (purchase), total revenue.
Customize the report to add those columns and remove ones nobody reads.
Save the report so future reads start from this template.

test.method: Time how long a recurring read takes before and after saving the template
test.measure: time to produce the same read

title: Judge landing pages in the Landing page report, never by revenue in Pages and screens
hypothesis: If page value questions use the Landing page report instead of Pages and screens, then revenue stops piling onto the checkout page by mistake.

signal.check: A page's value is being judged from Pages and screens revenue, which credits the page where the purchase happened rather than where the session started.

risk.note: None.

steps: Open Reports > Engagement > Landing page instead of Pages and screens for any page-value question.
Confirm the homepage (/) sits at the top for a typical store.
Read revenue for a landing page as revenue from sessions that started there, not revenue from purchases made there.

test.method: Compare the same page's value in both reports
test.measure: size of the difference between the two reads

title: Read a checkout page showing as a landing page as a session break, not a real entry
hypothesis: If a checkout page appearing in the Landing page report is read as a session-timeout artifact instead of a real entry point, then nobody chases a fake traffic source for checkout.

signal.check: The Landing page report shows meaningful sessions starting on a checkout page.

risk.note: None; this is a reading habit.

steps: When a checkout URL appears as a landing page, treat it as a session that expired mid-checkout, not a new visitor.
Do not build acquisition conclusions from this row.
If the volume is large, revisit the session timeout decision instead.

test.method: Track the size of this row over a few periods
test.measure: sessions attributed to checkout-as-landing-page

title: Rule out a traffic mismatch before blaming a product page for low conversion
hypothesis: If a low-converting product page is checked for a traffic mix mismatch before anyone touches the page, then the store stops redesigning pages that were never the real problem.

signal.check: A product landing page shows a lower purchase-filtered conversion rate than peer pages, and nobody has compared its traffic source and medium mix to those peers.

risk.note: None; this is a diagnosis step before spending on a fix.

prerequisites: Enough sessions per page for a stable rate
steps: In the Landing page report with the purchase filter, sort by sessions and note pages far above or below peers.
For a low page, add Session source / medium as a second dimension.
If the traffic mix differs from peer pages, treat the cause as traffic, not the page.
Only hand a page redesign hypothesis to testing once traffic is ruled out.

test.method: Compare conversion rate for the low page's top traffic source against the same source on a peer page
test.measure: conversion rate gap once traffic mix is matched

title: Use Explore for a single question, keep standard Reports for ongoing monitoring
hypothesis: If one-off questions go through Explore and only recurring checks live in standard Reports, then nobody drowns in an empty free-form table with no filter.

signal.check: A one-off question is being forced into a standard report, or an Explore free-form table is built with no event filter and returns a huge, meaningless total row.

risk.note: None; explorations are private until shared, and limited by retention.

steps: For a one-off question (revenue by country and device, site search terms), build an Explore free form.
Filter the free form to the event you care about before reading the first row.
For a question the team checks weekly, build it as a standard report instead.

test.method: Time how long a one-off question takes in Explore vs forcing it into a standard report
test.measure: time to answer

title: Keep indirectly followed by in funnel explorations and add a device breakdown
hypothesis: If a funnel exploration keeps indirectly followed by and adds a Device category breakdown, then step drop-off numbers are not accidentally shrunk and a mobile gap is flagged as a hypothesis, not a finding.

signal.check: A funnel exploration was accidentally set to directly followed by, or has no device breakdown despite a suspected mobile issue.

risk.note: None.

steps: Build the funnel exploration with view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase.
Confirm the step setting reads indirectly followed by, not directly followed by.
Add Device category as a breakdown.
Treat a desktop vs mobile gap as a hypothesis to check, not a finding to act on.

test.method: Rebuild the same funnel with the other step setting and compare
test.measure: difference in step conversion between directly and indirectly followed by

title: Treat GA4's AI answers as leads to check, never as findings
hypothesis: If every Analytics Advisor or Insights answer is checked in the underlying report before it is used, then a wrong date range or a repeated myth never drives a real decision.

signal.check: A GA4 AI summary or insight is used directly in a decision, a channel-kill call, or a client report without checking it against the underlying report.

risk.note: Acting on an unverified AI answer risks a wrong spend, reorder, or channel-kill call.

steps: Treat any Analytics Advisor or Insights answer as a lead, not a finding.
Open the underlying report and confirm the number and date range match.
Never let an AI summary alone decide ROAS, reorder, or channel-kill calls.

test.method: Spot-check the next 3 AI-generated answers against their source reports
test.measure: share of AI answers that matched the underlying report

title: Track and investigate the (not set) share instead of ignoring it
hypothesis: If the (not set) share of a dimension is tracked and investigated when it grows, then the store catches a tagging or timeout problem instead of reading unknown as if it were a real value.

signal.check: A dimension shows a large or growing (not set) share and nobody has looked into why.

risk.note: None; this is a monitoring habit.

prerequisites: needs brand data: baseline (not set) share per report
steps: Add the (not set) share as a column in reports where it can appear (landing page, channel).
Set a baseline from the brand's own history.
When the share jumps well above baseline, investigate session timeout, tagging gaps, or a new traffic source before anything else.
Read (not set) as unknown, never as zero.

test.method: Track the (not set) share over the next few periods
test.measure: trend in (not set) share against baseline

title: Use the Ecommerce purchases report for product calls and Checkout journey for technical bugs
hypothesis: If product decisions read the Ecommerce purchases report and technical checkout problems read the Checkout journey report with device and browser breakdowns, then each question gets the report built for it.

signal.check: A product-mix question is being answered from the Checkout journey report, or a checkout bug question is being answered without a browser breakdown.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: Ecommerce events confirmed arriving
steps: For item views, add to carts, purchases and item revenue, use the Ecommerce purchases report.
For checkout step problems, use the Checkout journey report with Device category and Browser breakdowns.
If one browser drops far more at one step, reproduce the checkout in that browser before calling it a real bug.

test.method: Reproduce a flagged browser-specific drop manually
test.measure: whether the bug reproduces in that browser

title: Read BFCM and flash-sale days day-over-day, not week-over-week
hypothesis: If peak-traffic days are compared day-over-day and the attribution window is widened before judging a holiday campaign, then a slow attribution catch-up does not read as a failed campaign.

signal.check: A BFCM or flash-sale campaign is being judged against last week's numbers, or judged the same day it ran, before attribution has caught up.

risk.note: None; this is a reading timing change.

steps: For BFCM, flash sales, or any peak-traffic window, compare day-over-day, not week-over-week.
Wait for the attribution window to close before scoring the campaign's final ROAS.
Flag any single day that carries an outsized share of the period's revenue or spend.

test.method: Re-score the same peak campaign at 24 hours, 3 days and after the full attribution window
test.measure: how much the ROAS estimate changes at each point

title: Send every Meta event both from the browser pixel and CAPI, merged by one event ID
hypothesis: If the same Meta event fires from both the browser pixel and the server (CAPI) with one shared event ID, then blocked or lost browser events are still counted once, not zero or twice.

signal.check: The store sends Meta events from only the browser pixel, or from both pixel and server without a shared event ID for deduplication.

expected_effect.size: unknown, not measured on a store

risk.note: Publishing a server stream before the dedup check passes double-counts every event until fixed.

prerequisites: Meta pixel already live
GTM web and server containers, or an equivalent CAPI route
steps: Confirm the browser pixel is live and firing on the events that matter (PageView, ViewContent, AddToCart, InitiateCheckout, Purchase).
Build the matching server-side CAPI event for each one, sharing the same event ID as the browser copy.
Never publish the server stream before the dedup check (searching for the shared ID in Events Manager) passes for every event type.
Once dedup is proven, keep both streams running together.

test.method: Compare Meta's reported Purchase count against store orders for the same 7 days before and after turning on CAPI
test.measure: ratio of Meta Purchase count to store orders
test.read_point: 7 full days after CAPI goes live

title: Prove Meta dedup by searching for the shared event ID, for every event type
hypothesis: If dedup is proven by searching Events Manager for the same event ID on the browser and server copy of every event type, then a broken automatic forwarding is caught instead of assumed fixed.

signal.check: Only PageView has been checked for dedup, or nobody has searched Events Manager for the shared event ID on AddToCart, InitiateCheckout or Purchase.

risk.note: None; this is a read-only check.

prerequisites: Pixel and CAPI both live for the event type being checked
steps: In Events Manager, open the detail view or Test events for each event type: PageView, ViewContent, AddToCart, InitiateCheckout, Purchase.
Search for the event ID and confirm both a browser and a server copy exist.
Confirm the server copy is marked deduplicated, not a green tag alone.
Watch for duplicate-event warnings or a sudden conversion jump in the days after.

test.method: Repeat the search for every event type after any pixel or server tag change
test.measure: share of event types with confirmed dedup
test.read_point: after every tag change, and again a few days later

title: Match both event name and event ID between the browser and server Meta copies
hypothesis: If dedup checks require the same event name and the same event ID, not the ID alone, then the store meets Meta's stricter documented rule instead of a looser one that can fail silently.

signal.check: A server tag's event name does not exactly match its browser counterpart's event name, even if the event IDs match.

risk.note: None.

steps: List each event pair's names on the browser and server side.
Fix any pair where the names differ (for example PageView vs Contact).
Recheck dedup status in Events Manager after fixing names.

test.method: Recheck dedup status for renamed event pairs
test.measure: dedup pass rate

title: Audit every live Meta integration before adding CAPI, and never run two server routes
hypothesis: If every Meta integration already sending events is listed before any new CAPI route is added, then the store avoids two server streams double-sending the same event to the same pixel.

signal.check: A Shopify Meta channel app, a GTM server container, or a CAPI Gateway could all be live for the same pixel and nobody has checked for overlap.

risk.note: Removing a duplicate route only stops that route; the other keeps working.

prerequisites: needs brand data: which Meta integrations are live on the store
steps: List every app or tool that could send server-side events to this pixel: platform channel apps, GTM server containers, a CAPI gateway.
Check Events Manager for more than one server route reporting the same event type.
If a platform plugin already sends CAPI, do not add a gateway or a second server route on top of it.
Keep only one server route per pixel.

test.method: Compare Meta Purchase count to store orders after removing a duplicate route
test.measure: ratio of Meta Purchase count to orders

title: Wait before calling a server-side Meta tag broken
hypothesis: If the team waits before treating a missing server event as broken, then a normal server delay is not mistaken for a failed tag.

signal.check: A server event has not appeared in Events Manager minutes after the browser copy, and someone is about to call the setup broken.

expected_effect.size: no figure given by the source; wait before concluding failure

risk.note: None; this only affects when to escalate.

steps: After confirming the browser event fired, wait before checking for the server copy.
If it still has not appeared after a reasonable wait, then check token, pixel ID and trigger wiring.
Log how long the delay typically runs for this store's setup.

test.method: Time the gap between browser and server event appearance across several test events
test.measure: typical delay in minutes
test.read_point: over the next few test sessions

title: Store the Meta pixel ID and token as constants per container, not shared across containers
hypothesis: If the pixel ID and access token are stored as constant variables recreated in each GTM container, then a server tag never fails from a missing variable that only existed in the web container.

signal.check: A server-side Meta tag fails and the cause is a pixel ID or token variable that only exists in the web container.

risk.note: An exposed token is rotated by generating a new one and updating the constant, not by editing history.

prerequisites: Business Manager admin access, or an admin who can generate the token
steps: In each GTM container (web and server), create a Constant variable for the pixel ID.
In the server container, create a separate Constant variable for the access token.
Store both values in a secret store, never in a doc, chat, or commit.
If Generate access token is greyed out, ask the account admin to generate and send it through a secret channel.

test.method: Check the server tag's status in server preview after wiring the constants
test.measure: tag status: succeeded vs failed

title: Use an exact-match custom event trigger for every server-side Meta tag
hypothesis: If every server Meta tag's trigger uses an exact match on the incoming event name plus the consent condition, then a name mismatch stops silently preventing the tag from firing.

signal.check: A server-side Meta tag never fires and the trigger's event name does not exactly match the name seen in server preview.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: Server container preview access
steps: Turn on preview in both web and server containers and perform the tracked action.
Read the incoming event name exactly as server preview shows it.
Set the trigger to Custom Event with that exact name, plus the consent condition.
Save and confirm the tag fires in the next preview pass.

test.method: Re-run server preview after the trigger fix
test.measure: whether the tag fires on the expected event

title: Map every store event to its Meta standard event with value, currency and content IDs
hypothesis: If every store event is mapped to the matching Meta standard event and carries value, currency and content IDs, then Meta's bidding has the signal it needs instead of a bare PageView.

signal.check: The store sends Meta events without value, currency or content IDs, or has never written down which store event maps to which Meta standard event.

risk.note: None; this adds data to existing events.

prerequisites: needs brand data: event map from store events to Meta standard events
steps: List the store's key events: product view, add to cart, checkout start, purchase.
Map each to its Meta standard event: ViewContent, AddToCart, InitiateCheckout, Purchase.
Add value, currency and content IDs to each mapped event.
Confirm each arrives correctly in Events Manager's event detail view.

test.method: Check Events Manager event detail for each mapped event after the change
test.measure: share of events carrying value, currency and content IDs

title: Read event match quality per event through the read-only Meta dataset tools
hypothesis: If event match quality is read per event with the read-only dataset tools and low scores are proposed as fixes for a human to apply, then match quality improves without the agent ever writing to the Meta account.

signal.check: Event match quality has never been checked, or customer information parameters (email, phone, external ID) are missing from mapped events.

risk.note: Read only; any fix is a proposal for a human to apply, never applied by the agent.

prerequisites: Meta MCP read access to the dataset
steps: Read ads_get_dataset_quality for the pixel to see EMQ per event.
List which customer information parameters (email, phone, external ID, IP, user agent) are missing.
Write a proposal to add the missing hashed parameters, for a Meta admin to apply.
Recheck EMQ after the fix ships.

test.method: Re-read EMQ a week after the proposed fix ships
test.measure: EMQ score change per event

title: Gate all Meta sending on consent where consent rules apply
hypothesis: If the browser pixel and every server trigger are gated on the consent-mode variable showing granted, then no Meta data is sent before a shopper has actually opted in.
does_not_apply_when: The store sells only into markets with no cookie consent requirement

signal.check: The pixel or a server tag can fire before consent is granted in a market with a consent requirement.

risk.note: Sending data before consent in a regulated market is a compliance risk.

prerequisites: needs brand data: markets served and consent rules that apply
A cookie consent tool with a dataLayer event
steps: List the markets the store sells into and their consent rules.
Add a Require additional consent for tag to fire setting on ad_storage for the browser pixel.
Add the consent-mode variable as a firing condition on every server trigger.
Test with the banner unanswered and confirm the tag shows blocked by consent settings.

test.method: Load the site with consent unanswered and check DevTools Network for any Meta request
test.measure: presence or absence of a Meta request before consent

title: Trigger a consent-gated pixel on the consent-update event, not on page load
hypothesis: If the consent-gated pixel fires on the cookie consent update event instead of Initialization on all pages, then the opt-in page view is not lost to a delayed first fire.
does_not_apply_when: The store sells only into markets with no cookie consent requirement

signal.check: A consent-gated pixel is set to fire on Initialization - All Pages, so it only fires on the page after the shopper opts in, not the opt-in page itself.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: A cookie consent tool with a dataLayer event
steps: Find the trigger currently used for the consent-gated pixel tag.
Change it from Initialization - All Pages to the cookie consent update event.
To retest, delete the consent cookie in DevTools and refresh, then click Allow all.
Confirm the pixel fires on the same page as the opt-in, not the next one.

test.method: Delete the consent cookie, refresh, opt in, and check whether the pixel fires on that same page
test.measure: pixel fire on opt-in page vs the next page

title: Keep the Meta test event code in a Debug-Mode-only lookup, never hard-coded
hypothesis: If the test event code lives in a lookup table keyed on Debug Mode instead of being typed into the tag, then a leftover test code cannot silently route real customer events into Test events.

signal.check: A server Meta tag has a test event code typed directly into its Test ID field, or the code has not been checked before the last test session.

risk.note: A leaked test code sends real customer events to Test events, where they do not count toward reporting or bidding.

steps: Create a Lookup Table variable with Debug Mode as the input, default value empty, and one row: true maps to the current test event code.
Put that variable in the Test ID field of every server Meta tag.
Before each test session, check Events Manager's Test events tab for the current code and update the lookup row if it changed.
Confirm a normal, non-preview visit sends no test ID and shows up in live data.

test.method: Check Events Manager Test events tab after a normal, non-preview visit
test.measure: whether any real visitor events land in Test events
test.read_point: daily, as part of the trust check

title: Do not expect the Meta CAPI Gateway to beat ad blockers or extend cookie life
hypothesis: If the team knows the gateway is a pixel plus a relay, blocked by the same things that block the pixel, then nobody buys it expecting blocker recovery or longer cookies it cannot deliver.

signal.check: Someone is proposing or has bought the CAPI Gateway specifically to beat ad blockers or extend cookie lifetime.

expected_effect.size: with an ad blocker active, neither the Facebook request nor the gateway request fired in one test

risk.note: None; this is a decision check, not a build.

steps: Before buying or building a CAPI gateway, write down what problem it is meant to solve.
If the goal is beating ad blockers or extending cookie life, know the gateway cannot do either; it accepts only Meta events and needs the browser pixel to trigger it.
Redirect blocker-resistance goals to a server-side GTM build instead.

test.method: Install an ad blocker, reload the site, and check whether the gateway request fires
test.measure: gateway request present or blocked
test.read_point: before deciding to buy the gateway

title: Treat Meta's gateway lift numbers and any vendor's counter-estimate as unproven claims
hypothesis: If neither Meta's claimed lift nor a vendor's smaller counter-estimate is put into a business case as a real number, then a CAPI decision is not made on an unmeasured figure from either side.

signal.check: A CAPI or gateway proposal cites Meta's up to 13 percent cost-per-result or 7 percent conversion lift, or a vendor's 1 to 2 percent estimate, as an expected result.

expected_effect.size: Meta claims up to 13 percent better cost per result and 7 percent more conversions; one vendor estimates at best 1 to 2 percent against blockers; neither is measured on a store

risk.note: None; this only affects what number goes into a business case.

steps: Cite both Meta's claimed lift and any vendor's counter-estimate with their source, never as a promise.
Put no lift number into a spend or budget business case.
If the store tests any CAPI route, measure a real before-and-after in Events Manager instead of relying on either claim.

test.method: Compare Events Manager event counts, match rate and ROAS for 2 to 4 weeks before and after a CAPI change
test.measure: actual change in cost per result and ROAS

title: Use a 3-condition test to decide between the CAPI Gateway and server-side GTM
hypothesis: If the store only chooses the gateway when it has no developer, no platform app already sending CAPI, and blocker resistance is not the goal, then it does not pay for a stopgap it did not need.

signal.check: The store is deciding between a CAPI gateway and building server-side GTM, without checking developer access, existing platform CAPI, and the blocker-resistance goal.

risk.note: A gateway can be swapped for server-side GTM later; log it as a stopgap with a review date if chosen.

prerequisites: needs brand data: store platform, how the pixel was installed, whether CAPI is already active
steps: Check all 3 conditions: no developer or server-side skill on the team, no platform app already sending CAPI, and blocker resistance is not the goal.
If all 3 hold, the gateway is a reasonable low-tech choice; write it down as a stopgap with a review date.
If any condition fails, build or commission server-side GTM instead.
Log the decision and the date.

test.method: Revisit the decision at the logged review date
test.measure: whether the conditions still hold

title: If the gateway is chosen, set up a dedicated subdomain and wait before testing
hypothesis: If the gateway is built on a subdomain used by nothing else, with the CNAME proxy off, and testing waits until DNS is live, then setup problems do not get mistaken for a broken gateway.

signal.check: R57's 3 conditions hold and the store is setting up a CAPI Gateway.

expected_effect.size: subdomain went live in 5 to 10 minutes in one test, up to about 1 hour for others; gateway cost about 10 dollars a month with a 7 day trial in one case

risk.note: Disconnecting the pixel in the gateway and removing the CNAME reverts to the pixel working as before.

prerequisites: R57's 3 conditions confirmed
needs brand data: who manages DNS and where
Business Manager admin access
steps: Baseline: check DevTools Network for a plain Facebook request and PageView before any change.
Sign up for the gateway service, connect the pixel, and pick a subdomain used by nothing else.
At the DNS provider, add a CNAME for that subdomain pointing to the gateway, with any proxy turned off.
Wait for the subdomain to go live before testing, then verify dedup and run the ad-blocker test.

test.method: Run the dedup check and the ad-blocker test after the subdomain shows optimized
test.measure: dedup pass and blocker behavior

title: Treat server-side GTM's extra features as unquantified, not a guaranteed upgrade
hypothesis: If a custom loader and cookie lifetime extension are named as unmeasured extras rather than a promised improvement, then the business case for server-side GTM over the gateway is not built on a number nobody has.

signal.check: A pitch for server-side GTM over the gateway cites a custom loader or cookie extension benefit with a specific number attached.

expected_effect.size: no numbers given by either source

risk.note: None.

steps: List what server-side GTM adds beyond the gateway: a custom loader that changes the request URL, and cookie lifetime extension.
Note that neither benefit is quantified by any source here.
If the brand wants a number, measure cookie lifetime and click-to-conversion match rate before and after, rather than assuming a lift.

test.method: Compare match rate and cookie-based conversion tracking for 2 weeks before and after moving to server-side GTM
test.measure: match rate change

title: Audit Shopify's native checkout tracking routes before adding anything on top
hypothesis: If the store audits what the Google & YouTube app, the Meta channel app and Web Pixels customer events already send before adding a new pixel or CAPI route, then nothing gets double-installed on checkout.

signal.check: GTM is assumed to cover checkout on a Shopify store, or nobody has checked what the platform's own apps already send on checkout and thank-you pages.

risk.note: None; this is an audit.

prerequisites: needs brand data: store platform, Shopify plan, checkout domain, apps installed
steps: List every app that could send checkout or purchase events: Google & YouTube app, Meta channel app, Web Pixels customer events.
Check what each one actually sends using DebugView, Pixel Helper, or the app's own reporting.
Confirm GTM is used only for storefront pages, not assumed to cover checkout.
Document the route for each page type before adding any new tracking.

test.method: Walk a full purchase and note which app reported which event
test.measure: coverage of checkout and purchase events by route

title: Cross-check Shopify sessions and conversion rate against GA4 before acting on either
hypothesis: If Shopify's sessions and conversion rate are checked against GA4 for the same days before a decision, then a bot spike invisible to Shopify does not drive a false conclusion about traffic or conversion.

signal.check: A Shopify conversion rate move is being acted on without comparing GA4 sessions for the same days.

risk.note: None; this is a cross-check before acting.

prerequisites: GA4 sessions available for the same dates
steps: Plot Shopify sessions and GA4 sessions by day for the period in question.
Flag any day where Shopify shows a spike or dip that GA4 does not.
Recompute conversion rate using GA4 sessions as the denominator for those days.
Report both rates with their denominator named.

test.method: Compare the 2 conversion rate reads for the flagged days
test.measure: size of the gap between Shopify-denominator and GA4-denominator rates
test.read_point: before acting on the conversion move

title: Never use Shopify's built-in attribution or referral cards as evidence for a budget move
hypothesis: If Shopify's attribution and referral cards (sales by social referral, sessions by referrer) are dropped as decision evidence and treated at most as one weak signal, then budget moves stop resting on a metric even Shopify's own presenter calls unreliable.

signal.check: A channel-kill or budget-shift decision cites a Shopify attribution or social referral card as its evidence.

risk.note: None; this changes what counts as evidence, not the dashboard itself.

steps: Stop citing Shopify's total sales by social referral, sessions by referrer, or similar attribution cards in any budget report.
If used at all, label them a low-trust signal alongside GA4 and UTM data, never as standalone proof.
Replace the removed cards on the dashboard with net sales, shipping charges, sessions, conversion rate, AOV and the funnel.

test.method: Check the last 3 budget decisions for whether Shopify attribution cards were cited
test.measure: number of decisions that cited them
test.read_point: review of the last quarter's decisions

title: Filter Shopify reports to the Online Store channel before judging paid media
hypothesis: If Shopify sales and session reports are filtered to the Online Store channel before judging paid media, then POS, Shop app and draft order sales stop blending into a paid-media efficiency read.
does_not_apply_when: The store sells only through its own Online Store channel

signal.check: A paid media performance read uses total Shopify sales without filtering to the Online Store channel, while the store also sells through POS, Shop app or draft orders.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: needs brand data: sales by channel
steps: Check whether the store sells on more than one channel: POS, Shop app, draft orders, Online Store.
If so, filter the Shopify report to Online Store before pulling any number used to judge paid media.
Report blended totals separately, labelled as blended, when they are needed for another purpose.

test.method: Compare a paid media ROAS read with and without the channel filter
test.measure: size of the difference
test.read_point: before the next paid media decision

title: Confirm Shopify Analytics order count matches store order count before trusting either
hypothesis: If Shopify Analytics orders are checked against the store's own order count, channel-filtered, then a mismatch is caught before either number is used in a report.

signal.check: Shopify Analytics order count and the store's own order export have never been compared for the same period and channel filter.

risk.note: None; this is a comparison check.

prerequisites: Order export with channel field
steps: Pull Shopify Analytics order count for a period, filtered to Online Store.
Pull the store's own order count for the same period and channel.
Compare the two; a difference points to a channel filter mismatch or a data delay, not a real gap in orders.
Log the result as part of the regular reconciliation check.

test.method: Repeat the comparison for the next reporting period
test.measure: size of the gap between the two counts

title: Read repeat customer behavior from the full cohort report, not Shopify's returning customer rate
hypothesis: If loyalty and repeat behavior are read from the full cohort analysis report instead of Shopify's returning customer rate, then a loyalty number stops rising just because new-customer acquisition slowed.

signal.check: A loyalty or retention claim is based on Shopify's returning customer rate card, which moves with acquisition volume, not real repeat behavior.

risk.note: None; this changes the report used, not customer behavior.

steps: Stop citing Shopify's returning customer rate as a loyalty metric.
Open the full cohort analysis report instead.
Build a new-vs-returning revenue split from the cohort data, not from the returning customer rate card.
Hand the detailed cohort and LTV formulas to the finance track.

test.method: Compare the returning customer rate trend against the cohort-based repeat rate over the same periods
test.measure: whether the two tell different stories during a change in acquisition volume

title: Report AOV including shipping when shipping is a notable share of revenue
hypothesis: If AOV is reported with shipping added back on top of Shopify's shipping-excluded figure, then the real order value is not understated when shipping is a meaningful share of revenue.

signal.check: Shopify's AOV figure is used as the real order value without checking what share of revenue shipping charges represent.

expected_effect.size: one example client's real AOV was about 7 percent higher once shipping was added

risk.note: None; this is a reporting adjustment.

prerequisites: needs brand data: shipping charges as a share of revenue; AOV distribution
steps: Pull shipping charges as a share of revenue for a recent period.
If it is a notable share, report AOV as (net sales plus shipping) divided by orders, alongside Shopify's own figure.
Look at the AOV distribution and new-vs-returning AOV before acting on the average alone.

test.method: Recompute AOV with and without shipping for the last period
test.measure: percentage difference between the two figures

title: Write one UTM convention and apply it to every paid and owned link
hypothesis: If the store writes one UTM convention covering Meta, Google, affiliate, influencer, email and SMS links and applies it everywhere, then medium and campaign reads stop being only as good as whichever link happened to get tagged.

signal.check: No single written UTM convention exists, or some paid or owned links (affiliate, influencer, SMS) are untagged while others follow different naming.

risk.note: None.

steps: Write one UTM naming convention: source, medium and campaign values for Meta, Google, affiliate, influencer, email and SMS.
Store the convention in the brand record so every link-maker uses the same values.
Apply it going forward to every new paid and owned link the store sends.

test.method: Sample 10 recent links across channels and check convention compliance
test.measure: share of links matching the convention
test.read_point: 1 month after the convention is written

title: Audit existing links against the UTM convention and fix the mismatches
hypothesis: If existing campaign, source and medium values are exported and checked against the written convention, then typos and missing mediums stop quietly breaking channel reports that already exist.

signal.check: A UTM convention exists but nobody has checked past or current links against it for typos, wrong case, or missing medium.

risk.note: None; fixing tags on live links does not affect past collected data.

prerequisites: A written UTM convention
steps: Build an exploration listing Session campaign, source and medium with sessions and revenue.
Export it and compare every value against the convention in code.
List mismatches: typos, wrong case, missing medium, paid social landing in the wrong channel group.
Fix the live links and note which historical rows stay mismatched.

test.method: Re-run the export a month after fixes ship
test.measure: number of remaining mismatches

title: Filter out fake organic and direct rows before reading a campaign table
hypothesis: If campaign tables filter out rows like (organic) and (direct) with a regex, then only real named campaigns are left to judge.

signal.check: A campaign-level table includes rows like (organic), (direct) or (not set) mixed in with real campaign names.

risk.note: Check the regex does not accidentally hide a real campaign named in parentheses.

prerequisites: UTM convention that never starts a real campaign name with an open parenthesis
steps: Build the campaign Explore table with Session campaign, source, medium, sessions, key events and revenue.
Add a filter: Session campaign Does Not Match Regex the pattern for parenthesis-wrapped values.
Confirm no real campaign is hidden by the filter.

test.method: Check the filtered table against the unfiltered one for any missing real campaign
test.measure: number of real campaigns accidentally excluded
test.read_point: when the filter is first applied

title: Check where paid social lands in GA4's default channel groups
hypothesis: If the team checks where Facebook and Instagram traffic lands by default (Organic Social) and fixes the medium or channel group, then paid social spend is not read as if it were organic.

signal.check: Paid social traffic is showing under Organic Social in Traffic acquisition instead of its own paid channel row.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: UTM convention in place
steps: Check Admin > Channel groups for where the default rules place Facebook, Instagram and LinkedIn traffic.
Confirm the brand's paid social links use a medium value that routes correctly.
If needed, create a custom channel group on a brand decision, and log it.

test.method: Check Traffic acquisition after the fix for a paid social row separate from Organic Social
test.measure: sessions correctly split between paid and organic social

title: Report the Last Click vs Data Driven attribution gap per channel, never one model as truth
hypothesis: If Last Click and Data Driven credit are reported side by side per channel instead of picking one as correct, then a channel is not cut or scaled on a model artifact.

signal.check: A budget decision cites only one attribution model's credit per channel, without showing the other model's number next to it.

risk.note: None; this is a reporting change.

prerequisites: Google Ads linked if paid search matters
Key events set to purchase
steps: Open Advertising > Key event attribution models with the key event selector set to purchase only.
Export channels with key events and revenue under both Last Click and Data Driven, plus the percent difference.
Report the gap per channel; state plainly that a large gap is a signal about the channel, not a measurement of true incremental value.
Route any spend reallocation through an incrementality test rather than the gap alone.

test.method: Track the reported gap per channel over several periods
test.measure: size and direction of the gap by channel

title: Write and apply one rule for when survey-reported source overrides platform credit
hypothesis: If the brand writes one dated rule for when a post-purchase survey answer is trusted over platform-reported source, then every future conflict is resolved the same way instead of case by case.

signal.check: The store runs a post-purchase how did you hear about us survey, but has no written rule for when its answers override or supplement platform-attributed source.

risk.note: None; the rule can be revised as more data comes in.

prerequisites: needs brand data: survey answers and platform credit for the same buyers and window
A post-purchase survey tool in place
steps: Export survey answers and the platform-credited source for the same buyers and window.
Compute the gap per channel in code.
Write the rule: which view is used for which type of decision, keeping budget on channels customers name that platforms cannot see, such as word of mouth or podcasts.
Record the rule and date in the brand record; do not cut an over-claiming channel on platform data alone.

test.method: Apply the rule to the next channel conflict that comes up
test.measure: whether the decision followed the written rule
test.read_point: next time platform and survey source disagree

title: Run a holdout test before reallocating spend on an attribution gap
hypothesis: If a channel's true value is checked with a holdout test before spend is cut or scaled, then a budget move is based on real lift, not on which attribution model happened to be shown.

signal.check: A channel is about to be cut or scaled based on an attribution gap alone, with no incrementality or holdout test run first.
