expected_effect.size: unknown; no method, volume, window or threshold given by any source here

risk.note: A poorly designed holdout can waste spend or give a noisy answer; route design details to the testing track.

prerequisites: A channel and outcome clearly defined
needs brand data: enough spend or audience size to hold out a segment meaningfully
steps: Define the channel and the outcome metric to test.
Hold out a random segment or geography from that channel for a set window.
Measure the revenue or order difference between the held-out group and the rest over that window.
Only scale or cut spend where the lift result supports it, not on the attribution gap alone.

test.method: Run the holdout for the defined window and compare results to the pre-test attribution gap
test.measure: measured lift vs the attribution model's claimed credit
test.read_point: at the end of the holdout window

title: Push zero-party survey and quiz answers into the CRM instead of leaving them in the tool
hypothesis: If survey and quiz answers flow into the CRM record for each customer instead of sitting only in the survey tool, then that data can actually be used for segmentation and retention, not just for a one-time report.

signal.check: Survey or quiz answers exist in a standalone tool with no connection to the customer's CRM or email profile record.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: A survey or quiz tool and a CRM or email platform that can accept custom fields
steps: List the survey or quiz questions currently collected.
Map each answer to a CRM or email platform custom field.
Set up the integration or export so answers sync automatically.
Confirm a test respondent's answer appears on their CRM profile.

test.method: Check a sample of recent respondents' CRM profiles for their survey answer
test.measure: share of respondents with the answer synced

title: Record GA4's attribution reporting model and lookback windows in the brand record
hypothesis: If the property's attribution reporting model and lookback windows are written down with a date, then every channel report cites the same known settings instead of an unrecorded default.

signal.check: Nobody can say what GA4's current attribution reporting model or lookback window is set to without opening the admin panel.

risk.note: None; this is documentation.

prerequisites: web check: current location and options for GA4 attribution settings
steps: Open Admin > Attribution settings and note the reporting model and lookback windows.
Record them, with the date, in the brand record.
Re-check and update the log whenever the setting changes.

test.method: Check the brand record against the live admin setting
test.measure: whether they match

title: Check GA4's attribution reporting matches the Meta buying window used for campaign decisions
hypothesis: If GA4's attribution settings are checked against the Meta buying window used for campaign decisions, then the 2 systems are not silently crediting the same sale on different timelines.

signal.check: GA4's attribution lookback window has never been compared to the Meta buying window (for example a 7-day click window) used for campaign decisions.

risk.note: None; this is a documentation and coordination check.

prerequisites: GA4 attribution settings recorded
The Meta buying window used for campaign decisions
steps: Get the buying-window attribution setting used for Meta campaign decisions.
Compare it to GA4's recorded attribution lookback window.
If they differ meaningfully, note the difference in the brand record so nobody expects the two systems to agree exactly.

test.method: Compare a channel's Meta-reported and GA4-reported conversions for the same period
test.measure: size of the gap explained by window differences

title: Reconcile GA4 purchase counts and revenue to store orders for the same dates
hypothesis: If GA4's transaction IDs are joined to store order IDs for the same window, then the gap between GA4 and real orders is a known, classified number instead of an assumed match.

signal.check: Nobody has joined GA4's transaction ID report to the store's own order export for the same time zone, channel and test-order exclusion.

risk.note: None; this is a read-only comparison.

prerequisites: Store order export with order id, timestamp, net sales, shipping, tax, refunds, channel, test flag
GA4 transaction ID report for the same window
steps: Fix the frame: store time zone, Online Store channel only, test orders excluded.
Export GA4's transaction IDs and the store's order IDs for the same 7 or 28 full days.
Join them in code; classify gaps as matched, in store not in GA4, or in GA4 not in store, with a likely reason for each class.
Compute coverage as matched count over store orders, and flag duplicate transaction IDs as a dedup failure.

test.method: Repeat the join for the next reporting window
test.measure: coverage ratio and count of duplicate transaction IDs

title: Compare Meta's Purchase count and value against store orders to catch dedup failure
hypothesis: If Meta's Purchase count and value for the period are compared against store orders for the same days, then a dedup failure (near 2x orders) is caught before it distorts ROAS.

signal.check: Meta's reported Purchase count has never been compared to store orders for the same days and channel.

expected_effect.size: near 1x orders is normal; near 2x is a dedup failure

risk.note: None; this is a read-only comparison using Meta's read-only dataset tools.

prerequisites: Meta MCP read access to dataset stats
Store order count for the same period
steps: Read Meta's Purchase count and value for the last 7 full days from the dataset stats tool.
Compare it to store orders and net sales plus shipping for the same days and channel.
A count near 2x orders signals a dedup failure; investigate the CAPI or gateway setup.
Document what the Meta Purchase value field includes (shipping, tax) once known.

test.method: Recheck the ratio after any dedup fix
test.measure: Meta Purchase count divided by store orders

title: Define revenue for marketing math as net sales plus shipping, tax out
hypothesis: If every marketing revenue figure is net sales plus shipping with tax excluded, and labelled that way, then ROAS and CAC math is not built on a number that also includes tax or unpaid orders.

signal.check: A revenue figure used in ROAS, CAC, or spend efficiency math is total sales (tax in) or gross sales, or is labelled cash collected without qualification.

risk.note: None; this is a labelling and formula fix.

prerequisites: needs brand data: net sales, shipping charges, taxes and refunds for the period
steps: Pull net sales, shipping charges, tax and refunds separately for the period.
Compute the marketing revenue figure as net sales plus shipping, tax excluded.
Label it net sales plus shipping in every report, never cash collected or total sales.
Take cash figures from the payments or finance report instead.

test.method: Recompute the last period's revenue figure with this formula and compare to what was previously reported
test.measure: size of the correction

title: Read a revenue dip for return timing before blaming ads or the site
hypothesis: If refunds are checked by refund date before a revenue dip is explained, then a return-driven dip is not read as a falling ad performance or a broken funnel.

signal.check: A revenue dip is being investigated without first checking whether refunds spiked in the period, especially in a high-return category like fashion.

expected_effect.size: one example: 20 percent of a strong month's orders came back the next month, faking a dip and a CAC rise

risk.note: None; this is a diagnosis step.

prerequisites: needs brand data: refunds by refund date and by original order date; return rate by month
steps: Pull refunds by refund date and by original order month for the period showing the dip.
Check whether refund volume spiked in the dip period.
If so, report the dip as return timing, not ad or funnel performance, and show refund timing as its own column, never as cash.
Never call an add-back of returns cash or profit.

test.method: Re-run the revenue read with refunds shown separately for the next 2 periods
test.measure: whether the dip disappears once return timing is separated

title: Break every revenue change into sessions, conversion rate and AOV before naming a cause
hypothesis: If any revenue move is split into sessions, conversion rate and AOV on one consistent basis, then the team argues about the actual lever that moved instead of a guess.

signal.check: A revenue rise or fall is being explained without separating the sessions, conversion rate and AOV changes behind it.

risk.note: None; this is a diagnostic method.

prerequisites: Store figures and a comparison period
GA4 sessions for both periods
Refunds by refund date and order date
steps: Pull net sales plus shipping, sessions, conversion rate and AOV for both periods, filtered consistently to Online Store if paid media is the driver.
Put all 3 levers on one basis in code: sessions from GA4, conversion rate as orders over that session count, AOV as net sales plus shipping over orders.
Check returns first; if refunds spiked, the dip may be return timing, not a lever move.
Name the lever that moved as a question to check, not an answer, and report normal variation when every lever moved only single digits.

test.method: Confirm the 3 levers multiply back to the reported revenue within rounding
test.measure: match between the computed product and actual revenue

title: Treat single-digit moves across several levers as normal variation, not a story
hypothesis: If small moves in AOV, conversion rate and sessions that compound into a bigger top-line number are read as normal variation when nothing moved sharply, then the team stops inventing causes for noise.

signal.check: A top-line revenue move is being explained with a specific cause, but every underlying lever (sessions, conversion rate, AOV) only moved a few percent.

expected_effect.size: example: a 5 percent AOV dip plus a 4 percent conversion dip compounds to about 8.8 percent, not the 10 percent a presenter called it

risk.note: None; this is a reading discipline.

prerequisites: The sessions x conversion rate x AOV triage already run
steps: After running the triage, check whether any single lever moved sharply.
If every lever moved only single digits, report no single cause, within normal variation.
Flag the period for a proper test only if the brand wants to investigate further.
Always recompute compounding moves in code rather than repeating a rough mental estimate.

test.method: Track how often no single cause reports later turn out to have had a real, missed cause
test.measure: share of no single cause calls that held up over the following period

title: Track unshipped orders as a fulfilment backlog signal
hypothesis: If orders minus orders fulfilled is tracked as its own number, then a growing fulfilment backlog is raised with operations before it shows up as customer complaints.

signal.check: The gap between total orders and fulfilled orders on the Shopify dashboard has never been tracked as its own metric.

risk.note: None; this is a monitoring addition.

steps: Pull orders and orders fulfilled from the Shopify dashboard for a recent period.
Compute the gap and track it over time.
If the gap grows, raise it with operations as a backlog, not a marketing or tracking issue.

test.method: Track the gap weekly for a month
test.measure: trend in the unshipped order count

title: Reconcile marketplace and omnichannel sales to their own platform reports before folding them in
hypothesis: If Amazon, TikTok Shop, Instagram Shop or a Shopping feed's sales are reconciled to their own platform reports before joining the store total, then a marketplace sale never gets blended into a paid-media efficiency read it does not belong in.
does_not_apply_when: The store sells only through its own Online Store

signal.check: The store sells on a marketplace or social shop channel, and its sales are being folded into the store total or into a paid-media read without separate reconciliation.

risk.note: None; this is a reconciliation and reporting change.

prerequisites: Each marketplace's own sales report or feed
steps: List every marketplace or omnichannel feed the store sells through.
Pull each one's own sales report for the same period.
Reconcile each to the store's combined total separately, the same way GA4 and Meta are reconciled to store orders.
Keep marketplace sales out of any paid-media efficiency read, alongside the Online Store channel filter.

test.method: Compare each marketplace's reported sales to what shows in the store's combined total
test.measure: reconciliation gap per marketplace

title: Find out and document whether Meta's Purchase value includes shipping and tax
hypothesis: If the store documents whether the Meta Purchase event's value field includes shipping and tax, then Meta-reported ROAS is compared against store revenue on a known, matched basis instead of a guess.

signal.check: Nobody knows whether the value sent on the Meta Purchase event includes shipping, tax, both, or neither.

risk.note: None; this is documentation.

prerequisites: needs brand data: what the Meta Purchase value contains
steps: Check the code or app setting that sends the value parameter on the Purchase event.
Confirm whether it includes shipping, tax, both, or is net sales only.
Document the answer in the brand record next to the revenue definition (R74).
Use this basis when comparing Meta-reported ROAS to store revenue.

test.method: Compare Meta's reported Purchase value to store net sales plus shipping for a known order sample
test.measure: size and direction of the gap

title: Pick one top metric, customers, revenue or profit, matched to stage and bankroll
hypothesis: If the executive team picks one top metric matched to the store's stage and bankroll, then every department frames its work against the same number instead of pulling in different directions.

signal.check: The team cannot agree, or has never explicitly named, whether the store is optimizing for customer count, revenue, or profit right now.

risk.note: The metric can be changed later; log the date if it is.

prerequisites: needs brand data: stage and bankroll
steps: Name the store's stage: still finding product-market fit, early growth, or a stable business with margin.
Pick one top metric: a hero-SKU or pre-launch store usually runs on customers; a catalogue store with margin runs on revenue or profit.
Record the date the metric was set and why.
Frame every report from this point forward on the chosen metric.

test.method: Ask each department which top metric the store is running on
test.measure: share of departments naming the same metric

title: Keep the top metric fixed for about a year; allow only short quick-win pushes
hypothesis: If the top metric stays fixed for about a year, with only short 2 to 4 week quick-win pushes allowed underneath it, then the team stops causing turmoil by swapping focus every month.

signal.check: The team has changed its stated top priority more than once in the last quarter, without a real stage change behind it.

expected_effect.size: review big shifts quarterly at most; the metric itself about yearly; quick wins 2 to 4 weeks

risk.note: None; this is a cadence rule.

prerequisites: A top metric already set
steps: Set a review date about a year out for the top metric itself.
Allow big focus shifts no more than quarterly.
Allow short quick-win pushes (review count, referral rate, loyalty points used) lasting 2 to 4 weeks without changing the top metric.
Log any change with a date and reason.

test.method: Count how many times the stated top priority changed in the last quarter
test.measure: number of changes

title: Move to the next lever once the current one shows diminishing returns
hypothesis: If the store tracks return per dollar on its main lever over time and switches focus once it flattens, then effort does not keep chasing a lever that has already paid off most of what it will.

signal.check: The team keeps pushing the same lever (for example conversion rate work) even though each extra dollar or hour is returning less than before.

risk.note: None; this is a prioritization habit.

prerequisites: needs brand data: spend and result by lever over time
steps: Track return per dollar or per hour spent on the current main lever over time.
Watch for the point where each additional unit of effort returns noticeably less.
When that point is reached, propose the next lever in the sequence (commonly conversion rate first, then AOV, then LTV).
Log the switch and why.

test.method: Plot return per dollar on the current lever over the last several periods
test.measure: trend line slope

title: List what a winning test could break before scaling it
hypothesis: If the metrics a winning test could break (LTV, customer quality, brand affinity, customer experience) are listed and watched before scaling, then a short-term win does not quietly cost more than it earns.

signal.check: A test won on its primary metric is being scaled without checking what it could do to LTV, customer quality, brand affinity or customer experience.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources note conversion rate or AOV wins can lower LTV, but give no measured example

risk.note: Scaling a winner that hurts LTV or brand can be reversed, but the damage during the scale window may not be.

prerequisites: A test with a declared win on its primary metric
steps: Before scaling, list the metrics a winner in this category has hurt elsewhere: LTV, customer quality, brand affinity, customer experience.
Set a watch on at least one of those metrics for the scale period.
If a watched metric moves the wrong way, pause the scale-up and review.

test.method: Track the watched metric for the scale-up period
test.measure: change in the watched metric alongside the primary win

title: When a HiPPO wants a change on opinion alone, propose a real test instead
hypothesis: If a highest-paid-person's-opinion request turns into a specific, runnable test (a hero image swap, a shipping threshold change) instead of an abstract test it, then the store gets a real answer instead of an argument.

signal.check: A page or offer change is being pushed through on someone's opinion alone, with no concrete test proposed.

risk.note: None; this reframes a request as a test, not a bet.

steps: When a change is requested on opinion alone, ask what specific, testable version of it could run.
Propose a concrete test the store can actually run: a hero image swap, a shipping threshold change, a headline change.
Route the test design and sample size to the testing track.
Report the result back to whoever made the original request.

test.method: Track how many HiPPO requests turned into an actual test vs a direct, untested change
test.measure: share converted to a test

title: Read funnel drop-off from add-to-cart onward as hypotheses, not conclusions
hypothesis: If a big drop from add-to-cart to checkout or from checkout to purchase is written up as a hypothesis (a suspect page or a shipping cost issue) rather than a proven cause, then the fix that gets tested is chosen with the right humility.

signal.check: A funnel drop is being reported as a definite cause (the cart page is broken, shipping cost kills purchase) without checking or testing it further.

risk.note: None; this is a reading discipline.

prerequisites: Ecommerce event coverage confirmed
steps: Read funnel steps from add to cart onward; a drop from session to product view is normal on its own.
For a big drop from cart to checkout, suspect the cart page as a hypothesis to check.
For a big drop from checkout to purchase, suspect shipping cost, trust signals, or a broken step as hypotheses.
Hand the hypothesis to the testing track instead of acting on it directly.

test.method: Check collections, navigation and search when product views are very low, before naming a cause
test.measure: whether the suspected cause holds up under a closer look
test.read_point: before writing up the funnel read

title: Benchmark cart-to-checkout-to-purchase against your own history first, then a general ratio
hypothesis: If the store benchmarks its add-to-cart, checkout and purchase ratio against its own prior periods first, and only then against a general 4:2:1 or 2:1:1 ratio, then a funnel fix targets a real gap instead of chasing someone else's number.

signal.check: The funnel ratio has never been checked against the brand's own history, or is being judged only against a generic industry ratio.

expected_effect.size: general average 4:2:1, low-ticket target 2:1:1; fixing a big drop lifted conversion 40 to 50 percent in one anecdote

risk.note: None; this is a benchmarking method.

prerequisites: needs brand data: funnel counts by step over several periods
steps: Pull the store's own add-to-cart, checkout and purchase counts over several prior periods.
Use that as the primary benchmark for whether this period's ratio is unusual.
Only then compare against the general 4:2:1 ratio, or 2:1:1 if the store is FMCG or low-ticket.
Never cite a single unverified example from an outside source, such as an unusually high add-to-cart figure, as a benchmark.

test.method: Track the store's own funnel ratio over the next several periods
test.measure: ratio stability and trend against the store's own baseline

title: Do not cite an unverified single-source funnel number as your benchmark
hypothesis: If a suspicious or unverified benchmark figure from an outside source is never repeated as fact, then the store's own decisions are not built on someone else's likely transcription error.

signal.check: A number that looks implausible on its face (for example a near-100 percent add-to-cart rate) is being repeated as a benchmark without checking it against the same source's other numbers.

expected_effect.size: a cited 99.2 percent add-to-cart figure is very likely a transcription error for 9.2 percent, based on the same store's other numbers

risk.note: None; this is a source-checking habit.

steps: When quoting an outside benchmark, sanity-check it against the same source's other reported numbers.
If a figure looks implausible, do not use it; use the store's own funnel history instead.
Note in the report why an outside figure was excluded, if it was clearly wrong.

test.method: Recheck any previously used benchmark figures for internal consistency
test.measure: number of implausible figures found and removed

title: Confirm every funnel step is tracked before reading a drop as customer behavior
hypothesis: If a funnel step at or near zero is checked for a tracking gap before it is read as a real behavior drop, then a missing event is not mistaken for a customer problem.

signal.check: A funnel step shows zero or near-zero volume while the step before it has real volume, and nobody has confirmed the event is actually tracked.

risk.note: None; this is a diagnostic check.

prerequisites: Funnel exploration or Purchase journey report
steps: Look for any funnel step at 0 or near 0 with volume before it.
Check DebugView or the event coverage table to confirm the step's event is actually firing.
Only read the drop as a real behavior issue once tracking is confirmed working.

test.method: Walk the step manually and confirm the event fires in DebugView
test.measure: event present or absent
test.read_point: same day as the flagged drop

title: Suspect bots when Shopify shows a spike or dip GA4 does not, or one city spikes
hypothesis: If a Shopify session spike or conversion dip absent from GA4, or a single-city spike, is checked for bots before anyone touches the site or ads, then a bot event is not mistaken for a real traffic or conversion change.

signal.check: Shopify shows a session spike or conversion dip that GA4 does not, or Sessions by location shows one city spiking against the market spread.

risk.note: None; this is a diagnostic check.

prerequisites: Shopify Sessions over time and GA4 sessions for the same dates
steps: Plot Shopify sessions and GA4 sessions by day; flag a Shopify move absent from GA4.
Open Sessions by location and sort by city; a single city spiking against the market spread often signals a server, not real customers.
Recompute conversion rate with GA4 sessions as the denominator for the flagged days.
Report both rates with their denominator named; if bot filtering is needed, note that Shopify may require a third-party tool.

test.method: Recheck the flagged days after any bot-filtering step
test.measure: change in session count and conversion rate

title: Treat very low engaged sessions on a channel as a relevance warning, not proof of a bad channel
hypothesis: If a channel's very low engaged sessions is checked for bots and mis-tagging first, then a real ad-to-page mismatch or a wrong search match is found instead of an unfair channel-kill call.

signal.check: A channel shows unusually low engaged sessions and is being blamed without first ruling out bots or UTM mis-tagging.

risk.note: None; this is a diagnostic check before a spend decision.

prerequisites: Bot check and UTM check already ruled out
steps: Rule out bots (R90) and mis-tagged campaigns (UTM audit) before blaming the channel.
For a paid channel, check the ad's promise (price, offer, product) against the landing page.
For organic, check the page against the likely search intent.
Treat any mismatch found as a hypothesis to test, not a proven cause of low sales.

test.method: Fix any found ad-to-page mismatch and recheck engaged sessions
test.measure: engagement rate change after the fix

title: Check stock status before blaming a page or funnel step for a conversion drop
hypothesis: If a product page or funnel step's conversion drop is checked against stock status first, then a sold-out SKU is not mistaken for a page or funnel problem.

signal.check: A product page or checkout step shows a conversion drop, and nobody has checked whether the SKU was out of stock during that period.

risk.note: None; this is a diagnostic check.

prerequisites: Stock status data by SKU and date
steps: Before diagnosing a page or funnel drop, check whether the product was in stock for the period.
If the SKU was out of stock, attribute the drop to stockout, not to the page or funnel step.
Route the actual stockout to the inventory and cash track.

test.method: Compare conversion rate for the same page during in-stock vs out-of-stock periods
test.measure: conversion rate difference

title: Run a daily trust check and publish a pass, warn or fail score before anyone reads yesterday's numbers
hypothesis: If a daily score across GA4, Meta and Shopify or store orders is published before anyone reads yesterday's numbers, then a broken source is caught before it drives a decision instead of after.

signal.check: The team reads yesterday's dashboard numbers without any daily check on event arrival, purchase integrity, Meta dedup, session ratios, or revenue definitions.

risk.note: A fail should block that source's numbers downstream until fixed or overridden in writing.

prerequisites: Read access to GA4, Meta Events Manager, Shopify or store orders
Thresholds and normal bands from the brand's own history
steps: Check event arrival volumes against normal bands, and flag any step at 0 with volume before it.
Check GA4 purchases and Meta purchases against store orders for yesterday, and check Meta dedup status.
Check Shopify vs GA4 session ratio and any single-city spike.
Check revenue definitions and settings have not drifted since the last log entry.
Score each source pass, warn or fail, and publish the score with the data before anyone else reads it.

test.method: Track how often a fail catches a real issue before a downstream report used bad data
test.measure: number of fails caught before use

title: Use Realtime only to confirm arrival after a send or launch, never for analysis
hypothesis: If Realtime is used only to confirm a campaign send or a site launch actually fired, and never used to analyze performance, then nobody draws a conclusion from a report built for a different job.

signal.check: Realtime is being used to judge how a campaign or launch is performing, rather than just confirming it fired.

risk.note: None; this is a usage discipline.

steps: After a campaign send or a site launch, open Realtime to confirm users and events are arriving.
Do not use Realtime numbers to judge performance or make a spend decision.
Wait for the standard processing window before reading real results.

test.method: Check that no report cites Realtime numbers as a performance conclusion
test.measure: number of reports incorrectly citing Realtime
test.read_point: spot-check of the next few reports

title: Log every settings change with a date and reason, and annotate reports across it
hypothesis: If every timeout, timer, key event, channel group, filter or consent change is logged with a date and reason, then a report spanning the change is annotated instead of silently misread.

signal.check: A setting was changed (timeout, timer, key events, channel groups, filters, consent) with no entry in a settings log.

risk.note: None; this is a logging habit.

steps: Create a settings log with columns: date, property or container, setting, old value, new value, who decided, why, reports affected.
Add an entry every time any of these settings changes.
Annotate any report that spans a logged change date.
Never edit a past entry; append new ones.

test.method: Check the log against the admin panel's actual current settings
test.measure: whether they match

title: Pair every quantitative drop with a qualitative check before proposing a fix
hypothesis: If every quantitative drop is paired with a session recording, survey verbatim, or support ticket before a fix is proposed, then the fix targets the real reason customers dropped off, not a guess from numbers alone.

signal.check: A conversion drop or funnel leak is being turned into a fix proposal using only quantitative data, with no recording, survey verbatim, or ticket reviewed.

risk.note: None; this adds a step before a fix is proposed.

prerequisites: A session recording tool, post-purchase survey, or support ticket log
steps: When a quantitative drop is found, pull matching qualitative evidence: a session recording, a post-purchase survey verbatim, or a support ticket from the same window.
Ask what this page or step is missing, using the qualitative evidence, before writing the fix.
Route the actual research method and interview cadence to the testing track.
Only propose the fix once both the number and the qualitative reason line up.

test.method: Check the next 3 fix proposals for whether qualitative evidence was cited
test.measure: share of proposals with qualitative evidence attached

title: Track one important on-site interaction GA4 does not capture automatically
hypothesis: If a store builds a custom GTM event and registers its parameters for one interaction GA4 does not track by default, such as a menu link or a filter click, then that interaction becomes reportable instead of invisible.

signal.check: A meaningful on-site action (a size guide open, a filter use, a menu click that matters to navigation decisions) has no GA4 event at all.

risk.note: Custom dimensions built for this cannot be deleted quickly, only archived.

prerequisites: needs brand data: theme's CSS classes for the tracked element
steps: Pick the interaction to track and find its CSS class, text, or URL pattern.
In GTM, build a trigger for that specific element using click variables.
Build a GA4 Event tag with a lowercase underscore event name and the parameters worth capturing.
Test in Preview and DebugView, then register each parameter as a custom dimension before publishing.

test.method: Build a one-off exploration filtered to the new event a week after launch
test.measure: event volume and parameter completeness

title: Store Meta pixel ID and CAPI token as secrets, never in chat, docs or code
hypothesis: If the Meta pixel ID and CAPI access token are kept only in a secret store, then a leaked credential in a chat, doc, or commit never happens because it was never typed there.

signal.check: A pixel ID, dataset ID, or CAPI access token appears in a text file, a chat message, a doc, or a code commit instead of a secret store.

risk.note: An exposed token is rotated by generating a new one in the same place and updating everywhere it is referenced.

prerequisites: Business Manager admin access, or an admin who can generate the token
steps: In Meta Events Manager, find the pixel and copy its ID.
Generate a CAPI access token; if the button is greyed out, ask the account admin to generate and send it through a secure channel.
Store both values in .env or a secrets manager, never in a playbook, page, chat, or commit.
Search existing docs and chats for either value and remove and rotate anything found.

test.method: Search the repo, docs and chat history for the pixel ID or token string
test.measure: number of exposed occurrences found

title: Test a new data source for 7 days before trusting it, then add it to the daily check
hypothesis: If a new pixel, app, GA4 property, or feed runs for 7 days in parallel with existing sources before it is trusted, then its definitions and gaps are known before any decision leans on it.

signal.check: A new data source (a new pixel, app, property, Metabase card, or affiliate feed) is being used in a report before its definitions, coverage and role have been checked.

risk.note: Removing a source from reports later is easy; the data stays available.

prerequisites: The new source's owner and purpose named
steps: Record what the source measures: its definitions for sessions, orders, revenue (tax and shipping in or out), refund timing, time zone, currency, refresh cadence, and who owns it.
Map its metrics to the ecomOS metric names; anything it cannot give is unavailable, never guessed.
Run the event coverage check, the dedup check, and the reconciliation check against it for 7 full days alongside existing sources.
Decide its role (source of truth for which questions, or a cross-check only), add it to the daily trust check, and log the go-live date.

test.method: Compare the new source's numbers to existing sources for the 7-day parallel run
test.measure: size and explanation of any gap

title: Propose sending gross-profit values to Meta instead of revenue so bidding optimizes on margin
hypothesis: If Purchase events carry gross profit (value minus COGS, shipping cost and payment fees) instead of raw order value, then Meta's bidding can optimize toward orders that actually make money, not just orders that are big.
does_not_apply_when: COGS per SKU and shipping cost per order are not yet tracked

signal.check: The store sends only order value to Meta Purchase events, with no COGS, shipping cost, or fee data folded in, while COGS per SKU is known well enough to compute margin.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source covers this, it is an ecomOS spec for review by finance

risk.note: Revert by rolling back the server tag version; never applied by the agent, only proposed for a Meta admin.

prerequisites: needs brand data: COGS per SKU, shipping cost per order, payment fees
Dedup and event mapping already working (R44 to R51)
20-FIN sign-off on the gross profit definition
steps: Define gross profit as value minus COGS minus shipping cost minus payment fees, using 20-FIN's definitions.
Draft the field mapping: which Meta field carries the enriched value, using the same event ID and name as the browser Purchase for dedup.
When COGS is missing for a SKU, mark that order's gross profit unavailable and exclude it from the value, reporting the excluded count.
Hand the draft spec to 20-FIN for review and to a Meta admin to apply; never apply it directly.
After it ships, run the dedup check, then 7 days of reconciliation with the value ratio, before reading any result.

test.method: Compare cost per result and ROAS for the weeks before and after enrichment ships
test.measure: change in cost per result and in the value ratio from reconciliation
